title: An army on the shore
hook: the war book opens with an embrace, a march, and God in human form awake by the sea
carry: an avatar weeps: God took on a human heart

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sita's jewel, a crow story only Rama would know, and your line: shravana, hearing the story again is devotion. Today the sixth book begins: the Yuddha Kanda, the war book.

The war book doesn't open with a war. It opens with a thank-you. Rama turns to Hanuman and tries to say what he's done: crossed an ocean, found her, come back. Then Rama looks at himself: an exile in bark clothes, living on a mountain, with no kingdom, no treasury, no land to give. So he says the one gift he has left is this, and he takes Hanuman in his arms.
screen: `NOT A WAR. A THANK-YOU.` → `NOTHING LEFT TO GIVE.` → `AN EMBRACE.`

segments.voice: Then the thank-you turns into a question. Hanuman crossed the ocean by leaping. An army can't leap. How will all of us get across? Sugriva answers like a good friend in a crisis: grief makes a person slow; let's march, and find the way when we're there. So the army pours south over hills and forests, Hanuman carrying Rama on his shoulders at times, and makes camp on the last shore of the land. In front of them, the ocean, roaring, with no far shore in sight. That night Rama can't rest. He speaks to the wind: you blow where she is. Touch her, and then come and touch me. Now remember who Rama is, for Hindus. He's an avatar: Vishnu himself, come down to earth. And look at what the avatar does. He grieves. He can't sleep. He doesn't know the way across, and he leans on a friend. That isn't a flaw in the story; it's the teaching. Hindus call Rama maryada purushottama, the best of men, living within limits. In this avatar, God doesn't skip the human part. He keeps his word, he loves, he weeps, he asks for help. Many teachers say that's why people love Rama so much: he knows a long night by the water from the inside.
screen: `HOW WILL WE ALL GET ACROSS?` · `THE ARMY MARCHES SOUTH.` · `RAMA SPEAKS TO THE WIND.` · `AN AVATAR WHO GRIEVES.` · then, large: `GOD TOOK ON A HUMAN HEART.`

segments.voice: Many Hindu homes keep a picture of Rama's court, the Ram darbar, with Hanuman kneeling at Rama's feet. Bring that picture to mind, or Rama holding Hanuman close. Then bring up one thing you're grieving or worried about right now, honestly, the way Rama spoke to the wind. If you pray, tell it to Rama, who knows that night. If you don't, just let it be named, and breathe with it.
The bridge. Setu in Sanskrit. Before there's a single stone, there's an army on a beach, and God in human form, awake by the water, asking how they'll all get across.
Your line: an avatar weeps, God took on a human heart. Tomorrow, Rama asks the ocean itself. See you tomorrow.

fork.reveal: Hindus call Rama maryada purushottama: in this avatar, Vishnu lives within human limits, and his grief by the sea is part of that.

what a scholar hears: Valmiki mostly lets Rama act as a man, while the Bala Kanda tells of Vishnu choosing to be born as him; later devotional retellings, like Tulsidas's, put his divinity at the center.

chat.meaning: As an avatar, Rama lived a real human life: he grieved by the sea and gave Hanuman the only gift he had, an embrace. Tears are part of the human life God himself took on.

Yuddha Kanda.meaning: the sixth book of the Ramayana, the war book

Setu.meaning: Sanskrit for a bridge or causeway

Sugriva.meaning: the monkey king, Rama's ally and friend

avatar.meaning: a descent: God come down to earth in a living form

maryada purushottama.meaning: the best of men, living within limits: a name for Rama
